findings.title: Row action buttons have identical, ambiguous accessible names across rows
findings.detail: In the Users table, every row renders <SuspendUserButton> whose visible label/accessible name is just t("admin.suspend") = "Suspend" (or "Reinstate"). The user's `name` prop is passed in but only used inside the toast/announce string (SuspendUserButton.tsx:33-34) — it is never surfaced on the button itself (no aria-label / aria-describedby). So a screen-reader user navigating by buttons (or the WCAG 2.4.4 / 4.1.2 "buttons with the same name must have the same/ disambiguated purpose" expectation) hears "Suspend, button" repeated for every active user with no way to tell which user each one acts on. The same applies to ReportCard's "Mark reviewed" and "Suspend the reported user" buttons, which repeat verbatim across every report card. This is confirmed by the test (tests/component/admin-dashboard.test.tsx:65) which can only query getByRole('button',{name:/^suspend$/i}) because the fixture happens to contain exactly one suspendable active non-admin user; with two it would match multiple elements. axe does not auto-flag duplicate accessible names, so the axe assertion passes while the real ambiguity remains. Note: provider/listener dashboards (e.g. provider session links) typically carry the subject name in the control's context; this admin table does not.
findings.suggestion: Give each row action an unambiguous accessible name that includes the subject, e.g. pass an aria-label like t("admin.suspendUser", { name }) / t("admin.reinstateUser", { name }) to the Button in SuspendUserButton, and aria-label including reporter/target on ReportCard's buttons. Add the corresponding keys to messages/en.json (keeping the visible short text via children while the aria-label carries the full context).

findings.title: Activity-table status badges expose raw enum tokens with no icon (machine text, color-only reinforcement)
findings.detail: The Sessions/Payments/Payouts tables render status via <Badge tone={...} label={r.status} /> where r.status is the raw database enum string — so screen-reader and sighted users see unlabeled machine tokens like "in_progress", "captured", "authorized", "scheduled" instead of human copy. This also violates CLAUDE.md rule 7 (all user-facing copy through messages/en.json) — note the table headers ARE translated (t("admin.colStatus")) but the cell values are not. Additionally, the local Badge wrapper (line 50-51) calls <StatusBadge tone> WITHOUT an icon, unlike every other status pill in the app (provider/PayoutsTable, IncomingRequests, customer/UpcomingBookings, and even the sibling UsersTable all pass an `icon`). StatusBadge's own contract says meaning should be carried by icon + text together, with tone as reinforcement; here a colored pill plus a raw token is the only signal, weakening the no-color-alone guarantee for distinguishing e.g. failed vs captured payments.
findings.suggestion: Map each status enum to a translated label (en.json keys) and a paired Lucide icon before rendering, mirroring PayoutsTable (t("provider.payoutPaid") + CalendarCheck). E.g. a STATUS_META record per table giving { label: t(...), icon } and pass both to StatusBadge so the cell shows readable copy and an icon, not the raw token.

findings.title: Admin user search has no live result-count / no-results announcement
findings.detail:
AdminUserSearch submits by router.push to /admin/users?q=…, which re-renders the server component and the table in place. There is no aria-live region announcing how many users matched or that none did. The DataTable's emptyText is shown but it sits in a plain , not a live region, so it is not announced after an in-place navigation. This is a regression relative to the codebase's own established pattern: app/(customer)/browse/page.tsx:55-56 wraps its result count in

{t("browse.resultsCount", { count })}

. A blind admin filtering users gets no feedback that the search ran or returned nothing.
findings.suggestion: Add an aria-live="polite" element to the users page showing the result count (e.g. t("admin.usersResultsCount", { count: users.length })) above the table, matching the browse page pattern, with a corresponding en.json key.

findings.title: Hardcoded user-facing string bypasses messages/en.json
findings.detail: The suspended-customer guard introduced by M13 returns a hardcoded English string: `return { error: "Your account is paused. Please contact support." };`. This violates CLAUDE.md rule 7 (all user-facing copy goes through messages/en.json). A suitable key already exists from this same milestone — `booking.suspended` ("Your account is paused. Please contact support to continue.") is used by the parallel guard in app/(customer)/actions.ts:26 via t(). The sibling createBooking guard does it correctly; only this new session-start guard hardcodes the copy. (The other hardcoded strings in this file on lines 47 and 85 are pre-existing, not introduced by this diff.)
findings.suggestion: Import is already there for t-style usage in the customer actions; reuse the existing key, e.g. `return { error: t("booking.suspended") };` (add the t import to this file as done in app/(customer)/actions.ts).

findings.title: Server action lets an admin suspend an admin / themselves; UI invariant not enforced server-side
findings.detail: UsersTable.tsx deliberately renders no suspend button for rows where role === 'admin' (and the test asserts this), establishing the invariant that admins are not suspendable. But the server action setUserSuspended only checks requireRole('admin') and validates the UUID — it does not check the target's role. An admin can therefore suspend another admin or themselves by invoking the action directly (e.g. via ReportCard's suspendTarget with an admin target_id, or a crafted call). Today the blast radius is limited because is_suspended is only enforced for customers in booking/session and is not checked at admin login, so a suspended admin is not actually locked out — but the data ends up in a state the UI treats as impossible, and the safety net is missing if is_suspended enforcement is later broadened.
findings.suggestion: After loading `target.role`, reject suspension of admins server-side: `if (target.role === 'admin') return { ok: false };` (optionally also guard against self-suspension by comparing userId to the calling admin's id). This makes the server enforce the same invariant the UI already assumes.

findings.location: SESSION_TONE / PAYMENT_TONE / PAYOUT_TONE maps + the status column render() calls (label={r.status})
findings.title: Admin activity tables render raw DB status strings as user-facing labels (bypasses i18n, inconsistent with every other table)
findings.detail: The three status columns render the raw database enum value directly: `render: (r) => <Badge tone={SESSION_TONE[r.status] ?? "neutral"} label={r.status} />`. So users see developer-facing strings like "in_progress", "captured", "authorized", "refunded", "scheduled" verbatim. This violates CLAUDE.md golden rule #7 (all user-facing copy goes through messages/en.json) and is inconsistent with the rest of the app: the customer account page already defines a localized status map (app/(customer)/account/page.tsx PAY_STATUS → account.payAuthorized/payCaptured/...), and components/provider/PayoutsTable.tsx / customer/UpcomingBookings.tsx render StatusBadge with localized labels via ternaries. The new code re-invents tone lookup maps but skips the label localization those patterns provide. Note also the trivial local `Badge` wrapper around StatusBadge adds nothing — other tables pass children directly to StatusBadge.
findings.suggestion: Make each TONE map carry both a tone and a message key (mirroring account.page PAY_STATUS), add keys like admin.statusInProgress/Captured/Authorized/Refunded/Scheduled/Completed/Paid/Failed to messages/en.json, and render t(key) instead of r.status. Drop the one-line Badge wrapper and use <StatusBadge tone={...}>{t(label)}</StatusBadge> directly for consistency.

findings.title: Dead message key: nav.providers is now orphaned
findings.detail: components/shared/AppHeader.tsx previously had the admin nav point at { href: "/admin/providers", labelKey: "nav.providers" }, and that was the only consumer of nav.providers. This diff replaces it with labelKey "admin.navApprovals" and removes nav.providers from the labelKey union type. Grep confirms no remaining reference to nav.providers anywhere in the codebase, so the key is now dead.
findings.suggestion: Remove the orphaned "providers": "Listeners" entry from the nav block in messages/en.json (or repurpose it if intentionally kept for future use).

findings.title: Suspension message hardcoded here but localized (t("booking.suspended")) in the sibling booking action added by the same milestone
findings.detail: This diff adds `return { error: "Your account is paused. Please contact support." }` for suspended customers. The same M13 diff added a booking.suspended key to messages/en.json and used `t("booking.suspended")` in app/(customer)/actions.ts createBooking for the exact same concept. The discrepancy is mild because session/actions.ts already had pre-existing hardcoded English error strings (it does not import t), so the new line is locally consistent — but it diverges from the i18n approach the milestone itself chose for the parallel suspension message.
findings.suggestion: For consistency within the milestone, import t and reuse a shared suspension key (e.g. t("booking.suspended") or a new session.suspended key) instead of a fresh hardcoded English string. If the team intends to leave session/actions.ts non-i18n for now, leave as-is — but then the createBooking suspension copy should arguably match that choice.

findings.title: setUserSuspended has no server-side guard against suspending an admin / itself (UI-only protection)
findings.detail: The UsersTable deliberately hides the suspend button for admin rows (`r.role === "admin" ? "—" : <SuspendUserButton>`), signalling intent that admins must not be suspendable. But setUserSuspended only validates `{ userId: uuid, suspended: bool }` and writes `is_suspended` for ANY target regardless of role — it even loads `target.role` but only uses it to decide whether to also flip `providers.status`, never to block admin targets. Server Actions are directly invokable POST endpoints, so any authenticated admin (the only caller that passes `requireRole("admin")`) can suspend another admin or themselves by supplying an arbitrary userId — also reachable via ReportCard's 'suspend target' button when `report.target_id` points at an admin. Impact is bounded (requires existing admin privilege; `is_suspended` on an admin currently has no login/dashboard lock-out effect since suspension is only enforced for customers), so this is not privilege escalation — but it is an unintended, server-unenforced state that the UI itself treats as forbidden.
findings.suggestion: In setUserSuspended, after loading `target.role`, return `{ ok: false }` (or a typed error) when `target.role === 'admin'`, mirroring the UI's exclusion. This closes the IDOR-style gap regardless of which UI path calls it.

findings.title: Suspension enforcement at session start is incomplete: only the customer-initiated path is blocked, and suspended providers are not blocked at all
findings.detail: The new guard is `if (profile?.id === booking.customer_id && profile.is_suspended) return error`. Two gaps in the brand-new suspension feature: (1) `loadBookingForParty` admits BOTH parties, so when the check subject is the provider (`profile.id === booking.provider_id`) the suspension check is skipped entirely — a provider can start the session for a suspended customer, who can then join the now-existing `in_progress` session, defeating the stated goal ('a suspended customer cannot start a call — protects providers'). (2) A SUSPENDED PROVIDER is never checked here: setUserSuspended flips `providers.status` to 'suspended' (which only removes them from browse / blocks NEW bookings via getApprovedProvider), but their existing `confirmed` bookings remain runnable, and startSession/endSession have no provider-suspension check — so a suspended provider can still run their pre-existing sessions. New-booking enforcement is sound (customer's is_suspended checked in createBooking; suspended providers excluded by getApprovedProvider), but the at-call enforcement does not fully cover either suspended party.
findings.suggestion: In startSession, after loading the booking, fetch both parties' suspension state and block the call if EITHER `booking.customer_id` or `booking.provider_id` is suspended (e.g. check `profiles.is_suspended` for both ids, or check `providers.status = 'suspended'` for the provider), independent of which party invoked the action.

findings.title: User-supplied admin search term is interpolated unescaped into a PostgREST .or() filter (filter-injection pattern)
findings.detail: `listUsers` builds `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)` where `term = `%${search.trim()}%`` comes straight from the `?q=` query param (AdminUserSearch form). PostgREST parses the .or() string as filter syntax, so characters such as `,`, `(`, `)`, `.` in the search term can break out of the intended two ilike conditions and inject additional OR clauses or trigger a 400. This is the only `.or()` interpolation in the codebase and is introduced by this diff. Security impact is low because the caller is always an admin (route guard + RLS `is_admin()` on profiles), so no data the admin couldn't already read is exposed — but it is a new unsanitized-input-into-query-DSL pattern that can cause unexpected filtering or errors.
findings.suggestion: Escape/sanitize the term before interpolation — at minimum strip or reject PostgREST reserved characters (`,()`. backslash, `*`), or wrap the value in double quotes per PostgREST quoting rules, or use Supabase `.ilike()` calls combined via `.or()` with properly quoted values.

findings.title: Reinstating a provider unconditionally sets provider status to 'approved', bypassing the approval/background-check gate
findings.detail:
`setUserSuspended` flips provider status with `status: suspended ? "suspended" : "approved"`. The provider_status enum has four values: 'pending', 'approved', 'rejected', 'suspended'. The action treats suspension as a simple approved⇄suspended toggle, but the target provider may currently be 'pending' or 'rejected'. Two concrete defects introduced by this diff:
1. Suspending a 'pending' or 'rejected' provider overwrites their real status with 'suspended', destroying the original state (no record of what it was).
2. Reinstating then sets status to 'approved' regardless of the pre-suspension state — silently auto-approving a provider who was never approved (e.g. one who hasn't cleared the background check, or was explicitly 'rejected'). This bypasses the M3 approval gate and is safety-relevant for a marketplace whose providers are vetted.
This is fully reachable from the UI: components/admin/UsersTable.tsx renders a Suspend button for every non-admin row (including pending/rejected providers), and components/admin/ReportCard.tsx's 'Suspend target' calls the same action.
findings.suggestion: Don't infer the reinstated status. Read the provider's status before suspending and, on suspend, only move 'approved' providers to 'suspended' (leave 'pending'/'rejected' as-is, or store the prior status). On reinstate, restore the saved prior status (or only un-suspend providers whose current status is 'suspended', mapping back to 'approved' only when they were approved before). Alternatively, gate the provider-status write on `target` provider status === 'approved'/'suspended' so pending/rejected providers are never auto-approved.

findings.title: Admin user search interpolates raw input into a PostgREST .or() filter string (latent injection / breaks on special chars)
findings.detail: `listUsers` builds `term = "%" + search.trim() + "%"` and interpolates it directly into `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)`. PostgREST parses the .or() argument as a filter grammar where ',' separates conditions and '(' ')' group them. Unescaped user input therefore (a) breaks legitimate searches — searching a name containing a comma or parentheses (e.g. "Smith, John" or "(work)") splits/garbles the filter or 400s, and (b) is a latent filter-injection pattern (an attacker-controlled value can append extra OR conditions like `,role.eq.admin`). The security blast radius is limited because the call is behind requireRole("admin") and targets profiles, which admins can already read in full via RLS — so there is no privilege escalation or data exposure beyond what the admin already has. Severity is low for that reason, but the correctness bug on normal inputs is real and this is the only .or() string in the codebase.
findings.suggestion: Avoid embedding raw input in the .or() filter string. Either escape PostgREST-reserved characters (wrap the value in double quotes for like/ilike and strip/escape internal quotes), or replace the single .or() with a safer construction (e.g. two separate ilike queries unioned in JS, or quote the pattern: `full_name.ilike."${escaped}"`). At minimum sanitize commas/parentheses/asterisks before interpolation.

result.reason:
CONFIRMED — real, actionable, and small to fix. Verified against the code:

- `setUserSuspended` (app/(admin)/admin/actions.ts:86-119) validates only `{ userId: uuid, suspended: bool }` (suspendSchema, lines 76-79) and writes `is_suspended` for ANY target (line 105). It loads `target.role` (lines 96-100) but uses it only to decide whether to also flip `providers.status` (line 109) — never to block an admin target. So an admin target (or self) is fully suspendable server-side.
- The UI deliberately treats admins as non-suspendable: UsersTable (components/admin/UsersTable.tsx:52-53) renders `—` for `r.role === "admin"` instead of a SuspendUserButton. That encodes clear product intent the server action does not enforce.
- A second reachable path exists: ReportCard.suspendTarget (components/admin/ReportCard.tsx:38-54) calls setUserSuspended with report.targetId, which can point at an admin — and the danger button there has no admin guard.
- Server Actions are POST endpoints, so any authenticated admin (requireRole("admin"), line 90) can pass an arbitrary userId for an admin/self.

Impact is correctly characterized as bounded (not privilege escalation): requires existing admin privilege, and is_suspended is only enforced for customers — at app/(customer)/actions.ts:26 (createBooking) and app/(customer)/session/actions.ts:51 (startSession), both gated on the customer branch — so a suspended admin currently has no login/dashboard lock-out. But it is still a genuine boundary-validation gap: the server permits a state the UI itself forbids, which violates CLAUDE.md Golden Rule 5 (validate role/ownership at the boundary), and it becomes a self-lockout / admin-vs-admin griefing vector the moment admin suspension gains any login effect.

Concrete fix: in setUserSuspended, after loading target (line 101), add `if (target.role === \"admin\") return { ok: false };` (or only when suspending), mirroring the UI's rule. One line, no schema change.

Confirmed real, low-severity. In lib/db/queries.ts:170-172 (new in this diff), listUsers builds `term = `%${search.trim()}%`` and interpolates it unescaped into `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)`. The `search` value flows straight from the `?q=` searchParam in app/(admin)/admin/users/page.tsx:17-18 with no Zod validation/sanitization at the boundary (which itself contravenes CLAUDE.md rule 5). PostgREST parses the .or() argument as its filter DSL, so reserved characters in the term (`,` `(` `)`) can break out of the two intended ilike conditions to inject extra OR clauses or cause a 400 — a genuine filter-injection pattern. This is verified to be the only `.or()` interpolation in the codebase and is introduced by this diff.

The severity is correctly bounded to low: requireRole("admin") guards the page and RLS is_admin() lets admins read all profile rows, so injected OR clauses on the `.from("profiles")` query cannot expose any data the admin couldn't already read, cannot pivot to another table, and cannot call functions. Worst realistic outcomes are a broadened/incorrect result set within profiles or a self-inflicted 400. The finding does not over-claim and its suggested fix (escape/reject PostgREST reserved chars or quote the value) is appropriate. Not pre-existing, not out of scope, not already handled.

CONFIRMED REAL and actionable. Verified against the actual code.

Location: app/(admin)/admin/actions.ts, setUserSuspended, lines 109-114:
  if (target.role === "provider") {
    await admin.from("providers")
      .update({ status: suspended ? "suspended" : "approved" })
      .eq("id", userId);
  }

The provider_status enum has four values — confirmed in supabase/migrations/20260605120000_m0_profiles.sql:9 ('pending','approved','rejected','suspended'), with column default 'pending' (line 42). The action treats suspension as a binary approved⇄suspended toggle, with two concrete defects:

1. Destructive on suspend: suspending a 'pending' or 'rejected' provider overwrites status with 'suspended', discarding the original state with no record of it.

2. Silent auto-approval on reinstate: reinstating hard-codes status = 'approved' regardless of pre-suspension state. A provider who was 'pending' (background check not cleared) or 'rejected' becomes 'approved' and enters public browse. This bypasses the M3 approval/background-check gate. Note the contrast: the legitimate approval path (decideProvider via the OUTCOME map, lines 14-21) sets status:'approved' AND bg_check_status:'clear' together — the approval gate. setUserSuspended bypasses that gate entirely by writing status alone.

Reachability fully confirmed:
- components/admin/UsersTable.tsx renders SuspendUserButton for every row where role !== 'admin' (line 52-56) — no status filter.
- app/(admin)/admin/users/page.tsx feeds it from listUsers (lib/db/queries.ts:167-179), which selects ALL profiles with no status filter — so pending/rejected providers appear in the table with a live Suspend button.
- components/admin/ReportCard.tsx suspendTarget() (lines 38-54) calls the same action on any report target.

The RLS guard trigger (supabase/migrations/20260605140100_m3_provider_guard.sql) does NOT mitigate this: it explicitly passes through admin/service-role writes (auth.uid() is null or is_admin()), and this action uses the service-role admin client.

This is safety-relevant for a vetted-provider marketplace. Recommended fix: read the provider's current status before suspending and stash it (e.g. a column or only transition when status='approved'); on reinstate, restore the prior status rather than unconditionally setting 'approved'. At minimum, only suspend providers currently 'approved' and restore to 'approved' only if that was the prior state — never promote 'pending'/'rejected' to 'approved'.

Confirmed accurate against the real M13 code. setUserSuspended (app/(admin)/admin/actions.ts:86-119) is new in this branch. Its Zod schema (lines 76-79) validates only { userId: uuid, suspended: bool }; it loads target.role (lines 96-100) but uses it solely to decide whether to also flip providers.status (line 109) — it never blocks an admin/self target before writing is_suspended (lines 103-106). The only guard is requireRole("admin"), so any authenticated admin can POST an arbitrary userId (including another admin or their own id) to this Server Action, and it is also reachable via ReportCard's suspendTarget button (components/admin/ReportCard.tsx:38-54) when report.target_id points at an admin. The UI deliberately forbids this: UsersTable.tsx:52-56 renders "—" instead of SuspendUserButton for role === "admin", so the server is genuinely less restrictive than the UI it backs — a real IDOR-style/UI-vs-server gap. The suggested fix (return { ok: false } when target.role === "admin") is correct and minimal.\n\nCaveat on severity (overstated as medium): impact is effectively nil. is_suspended is enforced in only two customer-only paths — app/(customer)/actions.ts:26 (block booking) and app/(customer)/session/actions.ts:51 (block starting a call). There is no middleware, no signin-time check, and no admin/provider login or dashboard lockout, so setting is_suspended on an admin is a functional no-op (not privilege escalation; the finding itself concedes this). It is a legitimate defensive-hardening / consistency fix but closer to low severity than medium given the absent real-world effect. Still a true positive: M13-introduced, not pre-existing, not already handled, in scope.

Confirmed real and actionable. Verified the full data flow with concrete pointers:

- lib/db/queries.ts:170-172 — `listUsers(search)` builds `term = `%${search.trim()}%`` and interpolates it unescaped into `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)`. This is the ONLY `.or()` call in the codebase (grep over lib/app/components returns just this line) and is introduced by the M13 diff.
- app/(admin)/admin/users/page.tsx:14-18 — `search` comes straight from the `?q=` searchParam, passed verbatim to `listUsers(q)` with no validation.
- components/admin/AdminUserSearch.tsx:13-19 — `q` is free-text from an `<Input type="search">` pushed verbatim into the URL; an admin can also hand-craft `?q=`.
- No Zod schema or sanitization exists anywhere in the chain (confirmed by grep across the users route, queries.ts, and lib/validation).

The technical claim is correct: PostgREST parses the `.or()` argument as filter DSL, where `,` separates conditions and `( ) .` are structural. So a search term containing `,` `(` or `)` (e.g. "Doe, Jane") breaks out of the two intended ilike clauses, producing either an injected/altered filter or a 400 — and because `listUsers` does `if (error) throw error`, a 400 crashes the admin users page on ordinary input.

Severity is correctly characterized as low for data exposure: `requireRole("admin")` (page.tsx:16) plus RLS `is_admin()` on profiles mean no row an admin couldn't already read is exposed. But it is a genuine, easily-triggered functional bug (user-input crash) and a new unsanitized-input-into-query-DSL pattern. Recommended fix: strip/escape PostgREST-significant characters (`, ( ) . : *` and the `%`/`\` wildcard chars) from the search term before building the filter, or split into separate `.ilike()` calls combined via a guarded helper, rather than string-interpolating raw user input into `.or()`. Worth fixing before merge.

Confirmed real and actionable. In components/admin/UsersTable.tsx:55 every non-admin row renders <SuspendUserButton userId name suspended>, but in components/admin/SuspendUserButton.tsx:40-48 the `name` prop is used ONLY inside the announce() toast (lines 33-34); the button's accessible name is just t("admin.suspend")/t("admin.reinstate") with no aria-label/aria-describedby (Button spreads ...rest, so one could be passed but none is). DataTable renders rows as plain <td> with no row-header association, so nothing ties the control to the subject user. Result: every active user yields an identical "Suspend, button" accessible name with no programmatic disambiguation — a WCAG 2.4.4 / 4.1.2 best-practice violation that is fully exposed in buttons/forms screen-reader navigation modes. Same pattern in components/admin/ReportCard.tsx:83-96: "Mark reviewed" and "Suspend the reported user" repeat verbatim across every report card with no per-card identifier on the control. The claim that axe does not catch this is correct (axe does not flag duplicate accessible names), so the passing axe assertions give false confidence. The test at tests/component/admin-dashboard.test.tsx:64 confirms the latent ambiguity — getByRole('button',{name:/^suspend$/i}) only works because the fixture has exactly one active non-admin user; a second active user would throw a multiple-match error. Given CLAUDE.md golden rule #1 (accessibility non-negotiable, screen-reader operability), this is in scope. Concrete fix: add a per-row/per-card aria-label (e.g. t("admin.suspendUser",{name}) -> "Suspend Casey") to each control. One nuance: a SR user reading cell-by-cell does hear the name in the preceding cell, so "no way to tell" is slightly overstated — but the duplicate-accessible-name issue and the fix are real and small, so it should be fixed before merge.

CONFIRMED REAL and actionable. The M13 diff adds exactly one at-call suspension guard in app/(customer)/session/actions.ts:50-53: `const profile = await getProfile(); if (profile?.id === booking.customer_id && profile.is_suspended) return error;`. Both gaps the finding describes hold against the actual code:

GAP 1 (provider starts a session for a suspended customer): startSession is reachable by BOTH parties. loadBookingForParty (lines 24-29) admits a user whose id matches customer_id OR provider_id, and there is a real provider entry point — components/session/ProviderSessionFlow.tsx (line 35) calls startSession, rendered by app/(provider)/provider/session/[id]/page.tsx via the provider's "accept" button. When the caller is the provider, `profile.id === booking.customer_id` is false, so the suspension check is skipped and the provider creates the in_progress session/booking for a suspended customer. No DB-level backstop exists: the M13 migration (supabase/migrations/20260608130000_m13_admin.sql) adds only the is_suspended column, a privileged-columns trigger, and a metrics view — no RLS/trigger blocks session creation for suspended parties. So the stated goal ("a suspended customer cannot start a call — protects providers") is only half-enforced.

GAP 2 (suspended provider not blocked at call time): setUserSuspended (app/(admin)/admin/actions.ts:109-114) flips providers.status to 'suspended'. getApprovedProvider (lib/db/queries.ts:52-64) filters status='approved', which blocks NEW bookings (used in createBooking, app/(customer)/actions.ts:41) and removes them from browse — but startSession/endSession never call getApprovedProvider or check provider suspension, and the provider session page (app/(provider)/provider/session/[id]/page.tsx:11-17) only calls getBooking + ownership check. So a provider suspended after a confirmed booking exists can still run that pre-existing session.

New-booking enforcement is genuinely sound (createBooking checks profile.is_suspended at app/(customer)/actions.ts:26; suspended providers excluded by getApprovedProvider), but at-call enforcement covers neither suspended party fully.

Recommended fix (pointer): in startSession (and endSession) in app/(customer)/session/actions.ts, after loading the booking, (a) check the customer's is_suspended regardless of which party is calling — e.g. read the customer profile via the admin client by booking.customer_id rather than gating on profile.id === booking.customer_id; and (b) verify the provider's providers.status is not 'suspended' (or that the booking's provider is still approved). This closes both the provider-initiated-for-suspended-customer path and the suspended-provider-runs-existing-session path.

GAP 1 (provider-initiated start bypasses customer suspension) — CONFIRMED. REAL, actionable correctness bug. Verified at lib/db/queries.ts:171-172: listUsers builds `term = `%${search.trim()}%`` and interpolates it unescaped into `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)`. The `search` value is fully user-controlled — it flows from the URL `searchParams.q` in the sole caller app/(admin)/admin/users/page.tsx:14-18 straight into listUsers with no sanitization.

PostgREST parses the .or() argument as a filter grammar where ',' separates conditions and '()' group them, and the ilike value here is unquoted. So a normal search term containing a comma or parentheses (e.g. "Smith, John" or "(work)") gets mis-parsed: `full_name.ilike.%Smith, John%` — the embedded comma terminates the first condition and `John%` becomes a garbage filter token, breaking the search or returning a 400. This breaks legitimate searches on ordinary human names, which is the real, actionable defect.

The injection angle is correctly characterized as low severity / latent only. I confirmed requireRole("admin") at app/(admin)/admin/users/page.tsx:16 is a genuine gate (lib/auth.ts:37-47 redirects non-admins), and the query targets `profiles`, which admins already read in full via RLS — so there is no privilege escalation or extra data exposure. This is also the only .or() filter string in the codebase, and no test covers this search path.

Fix: quote and escape the ilike values per PostgREST rules, e.g. `or(`full_name.ilike."${esc}",email.ilike."${esc}"`)` (escaping embedded `"` and `\`), or use Supabase's parameterized filter helpers instead of a hand-built .or() string.

Confirmed real, high-severity, newly introduced by this M13 diff (setUserSuspended does not exist on main).

The provider_status enum has four values: pending, approved, rejected, suspended (lib/supabase/database.types.ts:639). setUserSuspended (app/(admin)/admin/actions.ts:109-114) treats it as a binary toggle: `status: suspended ? "suspended" : "approved"`.

Defect 1 (state destruction): Suspending a pending/rejected provider overwrites status with "suspended". No prior-status column exists — the M13 migration (supabase/migrations/20260608130000_m13_admin.sql) only added is_suspended — so the original state is unrecoverable.

Defect 2 (approval-gate bypass): Reinstate hardcodes status="approved" regardless of pre-suspension state, bypassing the legitimate vetting path decideProvider (actions.ts:18, whose approve outcome sets status="approved", bg_check_status="clear"). A provider who was pending (never approved, bg check still 'pending') or explicitly rejected gets silently auto-approved.

Reachability is real and common, not an edge case: listUsers (lib/db/queries.ts:167) selects all profiles with no status filter; UsersTable.tsx renders SuspendUserButton for every non-admin row; ReportCard.tsx's "Suspend target" calls the same action. New providers default to status='pending' (m0_profiles.sql:42,89), so a typical not-yet-reviewed provider is exposed to this.

Impact is genuine, not cosmetic: browse (listApprovedProviders / getApprovedProvider, lib/db/queries.ts:37,60) gates only on status='approved' with NO is_suspended check, so reinstate-auto-approval actually surfaces an unvetted provider into discovery and makes them bookable; it also inflates the active_providers strategic metric (count where status='approved'). For a marketplace whose entire premise is vetted providers, this is a high-severity safety/correctness bug. Fix per the suggestion: store/restore prior status, or only map suspended⇄approved when the provider was actually approved (gate the provider-status write on current status being approved/suspended so pending/rejected are never touched).

The code builds `term = `%${search.trim()}%`` and interpolates it raw into `query.or(`full_name.ilike.${term},email.ilike.${term}`)`. Verified against the actual postgrest-js (v2.107.0) implementation at node_modules/@supabase/postgrest-js/dist/index.cjs:3021 — `.or()` does NO escaping; it just wraps the argument as `(${filters})` and appends it to the URL search params. The SDK's own docstring for the sibling filter() method explicitly warns callers "you also need to make sure they are properly sanitized." This is the only `.or()` string in the codebase, and no sanitization/escape helper exists anywhere in lib.

Correctness bug (the substantive part) is real: the `or` argument is PostgREST filter grammar where ',' separates conditions and '()' group them. A search term containing a comma (e.g. "Smith, John") splits the filter into garbage conditions (full_name.ilike.%Smith / " John%" / ...), garbling normal searches; a term with parentheses (e.g. "(work)") unbalances the grouping and 400s. So legitimate admin searches break on ordinary punctuation.

Injection vector is also real but correctly assessed as low blast radius by the finding itself: the `role` and `is_suspended` columns exist on the profiles table (verified in supabase/migrations/20260605120000_m0_profiles.sql), so an injected `,role.eq.admin` would append an OR condition — but the only caller (app/(admin)/admin/users/page.tsx:18) is gated by requireRole("admin") at line 16, and profiles are already fully readable by admins via RLS. No privilege escalation, no data exposure beyond the admin's existing reach. Hence Sev:low is well-calibrated.

Reachable trigger path: lib/validation/schemas.ts:115 defines reportSchema.targetId as z.string().uuid().optional() with no role restriction, and app/report-actions.ts writes that target_id verbatim. components/admin/ReportCard.tsx suspendTarget (lines 38-54) then calls setUserSuspended({ userId: targetId, suspended: true }) with no role gate — so a report targeting an admin (or a crafted direct server-action call) flips an admin's is_suspended.

Blast radius today is limited (as the finding states): is_suspended is enforced only for customers — createBooking (app/(customer)/actions.ts:26) and startSession (app/(customer)/session/actions.ts:51). lib/auth.ts getProfile/requireRole never check is_suspended, so a suspended admin is not actually locked out. But the row reaches a state the UI treats as impossible, and the safety net is missing if is_suspended enforcement is later broadened.

Fix is small and concrete: in setUserSuspended, after the target fetch, return { ok: false } when target.role === 'admin' (covers both suspending another admin and self-suspension, since the caller is necessarily an admin). This aligns the server boundary check with the documented UI invariant and CLAUDE.md rule 5.
